Time: 5 mins read 0 Add us on Google ₦210 trillion is not missing, we are told. It is merely unexplained. To an accountant, that is not comforting at all. This week, former NNPC Group Chief Executive Mele Kyari again insisted that no ₦210 trillion was lost under his watch, describing the disputed figures as bookkeeping issues. His former Chief Financial Officer and the former head of NAPIMS have made similar arguments before the Senate Public Accounts Committee. They are partly right: the figures in question are balance-sheet entries, not cash that walked out of a vault. But that defence misses the point. The question is not whether ₦210 trillion was stolen. It is why Nigeria’s most important commercial enterprise cannot explain what its own audited accounts say.
The facts are not in dispute. Reviewing NNPC’s audited financial statements from 2017 to 2023, the committee identified about ₦103 trillion recorded as accrued expenses and about ₦107 trillion recorded as sundry receivables. The accrued expenses, according to lawmakers, covered items such as retention fees, legal fees and audit fees without specific breakdowns, and NNPC linked part of them to joint venture cash calls. The committee rejected that explanation, noting that the cash call regime had been abolished with effect from January 2017. The receivables, NNPC said, were owed by defunct banks and other entities, yet no debtors or amounts were named. At about $117 billion, the receivables alone are larger than the economy of many African countries.
To understand why both sides can claim to be right, we must be clear about what these accounting terms mean, and this is where the public debate has gone astray. Accrued expenses are liabilities: costs the company says it has incurred but not yet paid. Receivables are assets: amounts the company says others owe it. Neither represents cash that has left the company. In that narrow sense, the former officials are correct that ₦210 trillion has not “disappeared”. But the narrow sense is the wrong test. The real test in accounting is whether a balance is supported by evidence. A liability nobody can itemise and an asset nobody can identify are not bookkeeping details; they are red flags. Consider the scale. NNPC’s former Chief Financial Officer told the committee that the company’s total revenue between 2017 and 2023 was about ₦54.5 trillion. He offered this as proof that ₦210 trillion could not be missing. Yet the same figure raises a harder question. How can a company accrue unpaid expenses of ₦103 trillion, almost twice its total revenue over seven years? How can it claim receivables of ₦107 trillion from debtors it will not name? Either these balances include large items that are not what their labels suggest, or they reflect unreconciled entries that have accumulated, possibly on both sides of the balance sheet, over many years. Neither explanation inspires confidence.
The first concern, therefore, is the quality of the accounts. Under the International Financial Reporting Standards that NNPC applies, receivables must be assessed for recoverability. A debt owed by a bank that no longer exists is, by definition, unlikely to be collected, and should be impaired. If ₦107 trillion of receivables cannot be traced to identifiable debtors, the asset side of NNPC’s balance sheet may be materially overstated. Equally, accrued liabilities must be supported by obligations the company can identify and measure. Unsupported accruals are not prudence; they are a failure of control. The second concern is the role of the external auditors. The committee chairman put the question bluntly: if reconciliation was not done, why did the auditors sign off on the financial statements? International Standards on Auditing require auditors to obtain sufficient, appropriate evidence for material balances, including confirmations for significant receivables and support for accounting estimates. Where they cannot, they are expected to modify their opinion. In July, the committee gave NNPC’s auditors one week to provide a complete schedule of every component of the receivables and payables, and rejected their claims of confidentiality. Auditors are paid to stand behind the figures they certify. Nigerians are entitled to know what evidence supported these balances and what opinion was given.
The third concern is governance. The dispute has dragged on for months, with written explanations rejected, summonses ignored and, in June, a warrant of arrest issued against Mr Kyari after he failed to appear. Whatever the merits of each side’s arguments, a public company that cannot produce a schedule of its own receivables after months of parliamentary scrutiny has a governance problem. The committee has raised other queries too, including about ₦5 trillion charged as direct production costs between 2017 and 2021 and an alleged ₦3.8 trillion duplication of subsidy deductions. Each deserves a documented answer, not a press statement. The fourth concern is the market. NNPC has signalled its intention to list on the stock exchange. After the success of the Dangote refinery offer, Nigerians have shown real appetite for owning shares in national energy assets. But no serious investor will buy into a company whose balance sheet contains ₦210 trillion of unexplained entries. Credible accounts are not a favour to the Senate; they are the price of access to capital.
What should happen now? Four steps are needed, and each addresses a distinct weakness this dispute has exposed. First, NNPC should publish a full reconciliation of both balances, itemised by counterparty, date and nature, with supporting evidence. This is the starting point because every other step depends on it. A reconciliation turns two aggregate numbers into a list of specific claims that can be checked: who owes NNPC money, whom NNPC owes, since when and for what. It would quickly separate genuine obligations, such as amounts due from joint venture partners or government agencies, from legacy entries that no longer have any basis. Publication matters as much as preparation. NNPC manages the nation’s oil wealth on behalf of all Nigerians, so its accountability runs not only to the Senate but to the public. Months of written explanations exchanged behind closed doors have not settled the matter; open disclosure would. Second, an independent forensic audit, by a firm with no prior relationship with NNPC, should verify that reconciliation. A reconciliation prepared by management is only as credible as those who prepare it, and the same institution produced the balances now in question. A statutory audit tests whether financial statements are fairly presented; a forensic audit goes further, tracing transactions to their source documents and establishing whether any loss, error or misconduct occurred. Independence is essential. Firms that audited or advised NNPC during the affected years cannot credibly review their own work. Only an investigator with no stake in the outcome can produce an answer the public will accept.
Third, the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria should review the conduct of the audits for the affected years and act where standards were not met. Audit exists to give users of accounts reasonable assurance that material balances are supported by evidence. If auditors certified ₦210 trillion of balances without sufficient evidence, the failure is not only NNPC’s; it is a failure of the assurance system on which investors, lenders and citizens rely. The Council is the regulator charged with overseeing audit quality. Holding auditors to account in a case of this prominence would send a clear signal to the profession and strengthen confidence in every audited account in Nigeria, not just NNPC’s. Fourth, any receivables that cannot be substantiated should be impaired and any unsupported accruals reversed, with the effect on past results disclosed transparently. Financial statements must reflect economic reality. Carrying uncollectable receivables overstates assets and equity, while unsupported accruals distort liabilities and past profits. Both give a misleading picture of the company’s financial health and of what it should be remitting to the Federation Account. Correcting the balances under the relevant standards, including restating prior periods under IAS 8 where the errors are material, would give NNPC a clean starting point. Disclosing the effect openly would show that the company is prepared to confront its past rather than bury it, which is the minimum any future investor will expect.

Ultimately, the issue is not whether ₦210 trillion was stolen; it is whether the national oil company’s accounts can be trusted at all. An entity that manages the country’s most valuable resource on behalf of every Nigerian must meet the highest standard of financial reporting, not the lowest. “Bookkeeping issues” on this scale are not a technicality to be explained away. They are a failure of accountability that must be fixed, transparently and in full, before NNPC asks Nigerians to trust it with their savings.
Posi Olatubosun is a UK-based academic faculty member in accounting and finance.
